For most homeowners, dripping faucets is the better and more practical option for immediate cold weather protection. Turning off the water at the main is typically reserved for extended absences or after a pipe has already burst. 

1. Dripping Faucets (Best for Occupied Homes)
Letting faucets drip prevents pipes from bursting by relieving the internal water pressure that builds up between an ice blockage and a closed faucet. 
	•	When to start: Most experts recommend dripping when temperatures are expected to drop below 20°F for at least three hours.
	•	Which faucets: Focus on faucets located along exterior walls or in unheated areas (basements, attics, garages).
	•	How much: A slow, steady drip or a "pencil-thin" stream is often more effective than a single drop every few seconds during extreme cold.
	•	Temperature: Drip both hot and cold lines (or set a single-handle faucet to lukewarm) to ensure water moves through both pipes. 


2. Shutting Off the Main (Best for Vacancies) 
Turning off the main water valve is the most effective safeguard against freezing because it removes the water entirely. 
	•	Requirement: Simply turning off the valve is not enough; you must drain the system by opening all faucets and flushing toilets until no water remains in the lines.
	•	Best for: Residents planning to be away for several days during a deep freeze.
You would fall under the #2 category and the flushing the system would be very important.
